text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game, figuring out how my points depend on tokens kept versus contributed, factoring in the negative externality on private keeping and the positive return from the group account.

Wait, I need to re-examine the rule — it seems each token in the group account pays 0.75 points specifically to the contributor, not shared among the group, which changes the whole calculation. Let me redo my points formula with that corrected understanding.

Working through the marginal math, keeping a token nets me +0.25 compared to contributing, while costing each other member 0.75 — so keeping everything is my dominant individual strategy regardless of what others do, even though full cooperation would yield everyone far more (60 vs 20 points). This is a classic social dilemma where individual rationality conflicts with collective benefit, and with no enforcement mechanism across the 10 rounds, there's no clear path to sustained cooperation.
